text:
“Take the earth!” from his high throne
said He who filled the void to men.
“To fulfill my sovereign purpose,
divide it among yourselves as brothers;
I give it to you as inheritance and domain.”


Each mortal hurried to answer the call,
each came first as best he could,
and took for his own all he could command:
the earth's fruits, the farmer;
the forest where the knight would hunt.


The merchant fills his barn and chest;
the monk takes the shadowed vineyard;
and the king, feeling strong at last,
marks roads and bridges off with barriers,
saying: “The tithe! The tithe is mine.”


Years later, when at last the irrevocable
division had been completed,
the poet came from a distant land.
Alas! Every field was bounded,
and every thing subject to its lord.


“Too late, in vain I ask my share!
Have you left the most faithful one in misery,
O God, and disinherited your son?”
Thus the poor bard said in tears,
prostrate before his Lord's throne.


“If, lost in the region of dreams,”
God answered, “you delayed, deluded one,
do not weep in vain or accuse me:
where were you, expecting me to forget you?”
“Where? At your side!” replied the dreamer.


My eyes were nourished by your beauty,
my ears by heaven's harmonies;
if I scorned earthly things on high,
it was your glory, shining without peer,
that held my mind and senses captive!


And God: “What can I do? On earth
nothing remains to fulfill your longing;
the forest and nearby estate are another's…
Come with me to heaven, if you please;
from today I shall freely admit you!”
